Current release: university prototype

What the demo shows today.

myhealth is a Flutter and Dart healthcare-management prototype developed at the University of Bahrain. The public demonstration uses synthetic information in browser-local storage. It demonstrates patient, staff, and administrator journeys; it is not a live clinical service or a certified electronic health record.

The questions behind the project.

The supplied proposal focuses on three practical needs. The report expands these into connected records, reliable scheduling, and staff coordination.

01 · Records and visits

How can one app organize health records and appointments?

Provide a timeline, original documents, clear source and review information, booking, visit details, and permitted family access. The report also explores summary organization and trends.

02 · Understanding and scheduling

How can patients understand their information and manage visits?

The proposal asks for plain-language PDF explanations. The report also studies schedule checks, repeated booking protection, reminders, and an experimental no-show model.

03 · Clinic coordination

How can teams organize daily work?

Provide role-specific schedules, charts, consultation drafts and signed notes, staff task history, and tools for administrators to manage clinic activity.

Objectives covered in the report

  • Organize related patient, staff, appointment, record, lab, medicine, consultation, and billing information.
  • Separate patient, staff, and administrator access, including checks below the screen level.
  • Track imported records, duplicate files, review decisions, and the origin of information.
  • Check schedules, exceptions, booking conflicts, and repeated requests.
  • Keep consultation finalization and related updates consistent; preserve later amendments.
  • Give follow-up work a priority, owner, state, and history.
  • Explore AI and prediction with clearly labelled synthetic evidence.
  • Support bilingual, responsive interfaces and maintain different levels of software testing.

Expected value includes easier access to information and clearer coordination. The project has not measured reduced waiting times, fewer clinical errors, improved health knowledge, or better patient outcomes.

A foundation built around clear responsibilities.

The interface, application rules, and data access are separated so that important workflows can be checked without relying only on a screen. These are implementation details, not claims of clinical approval.

What happens behind the main journeys?

Booking a visit

The app checks the selected patient’s permission, the clinician’s schedule and exceptions, and overlapping bookings before saving. A repeated request can return its original result. These local checks apply to the same database; separate browser databases cannot enforce one shared appointment allocation.

Uploading and reviewing a report

The app validates the supported file, records its date and source, calculates a SHA-256 fingerprint, and stores it with a pending-review state. An authorized clinician can review it. A matching fingerprint proves the file bytes match, not that its medical content is correct.

Finalizing a consultation

An authorized clinician saves a draft, then finalizes related notes, medicine orders, records, and appointment updates together. Signed content is preserved, and later changes use amendments. A software signature alone does not verify professional licensing or legal validity.

Issuing a medical document

A request moves through preparation, submission, approval, issuance, rendering, and delivery. The issued version preserves identity, language, issuer, and template details. Rendering is separate, so a failed render is not shown as a ready PDF. Real-world template approval and clinical policy review remain necessary.

Billing and notification work

Retries, payment states, and refund history are demonstrated without a live bank. Some local amounts use floating-point dinars; the report recommends a future migration to integer fils. Notifications enter a delivery queue, which records intended work rather than proving delivery.

Clear access. Clear history. Clear limits.

Role and patient-scope checks consider identity, current care relationships, accepted family links, and specific grants. Administrator access is not a blanket right to read every clinical record. Changing accounts should clear or ignore the previous account’s sensitive state.

Permissions

Protected operations are checked in repositories and the shared API, as well as in navigation.

History

Imported sources, review decisions, signed amendments, issued versions, and audit activity help trace changes.

Usability

Clear loading, empty, error, and status states; readable text; keyboard access; and Arabic layouts are part of the design goals.

The report targets 48dp touch areas, visible focus, screen-reader paths, and text enlargement to 200%. Formal acceptance with representative users is still open. The project has not supplied completed interviews, survey results, participant recruitment, or a measured usability study; its personas are illustrative.

Privacy and regulatory readiness need an independent review before real-data use. The report does not establish HIPAA certification, Bahrain legal compliance, or approval for clinical deployment.

AI research, with its evidence kept in context.

There are different kinds of automation in the project: example health summaries, an optional report-explanation gateway, predefined follow-up rules, and a no-show prediction experiment. These should not be treated as one validated medical AI system.

Report explanations

The supplied proposal describes an AI chatbot for uploaded PDF reports. The report records demonstration summaries and disabled live clinical AI. The current repository adds an optional server gateway that can return draft report explanations and follow-up answers with verified supporting quotes. It checks for missing support and reports incomplete coverage when only part of a long report is processed. This source update does not establish medical accuracy or clinical readiness.

No-show prediction

The report describes an 11-input logistic-regression model. Inputs include previous missed visits, booking lead time, first-visit status, a chronic-condition flag, previous appointment count, acknowledged reminders, visit hour and day, two visit-type indicators, and age. The output is an experimental probability and risk band, not an explanation of an individual patient’s behavior.

Developer-reported synthetic evaluation — not a clinical result
MeasureReported result
Held-out synthetic appointments2,145
No-show share25.1%
Accuracy0.733
Precision0.476
Recall0.623
F1 score0.540
ROC-AUC0.754
Majority-class baseline accuracy0.749
Confusion matrix1,236 true negatives; 370 false positives; 203 false negatives; 336 true positives

The baseline’s higher accuracy shows why accuracy alone is not enough. These results come from the report and repository documentation; they were not independently rerun for this website and do not show reduced real-world missed appointments. Operational no-show risk scoring remains disabled.

Rules and follow-up

Predefined checks can identify selected abnormal observations, medication gaps, or overdue follow-up and create accountable staff work. Duplicate-event checks, assignment, escalation, and completion history support the demonstration. The rules are not validated diagnosis or triage.

Scenarios the report asks the team to verify

Role-specific login; wrong-patient access denial; account-switch cleanup; valid booking; schedule and overlap rejection; repeated booking; file import and review; unauthorized PDF access; consultation finalization and stale-version handling; immutable documents; failed rendering; simulated billing retries; repeated risk events; no-show math and disabled capability controls; shared authentication; two-device booking races; Arabic and accessibility; a complete release run; and backup restoration.

For the graduation demonstration, show three complete journeys with synthetic data: upload and review a report; book an appointment and finalize the consultation; create or review a demonstration flag and complete its assigned staff task. Screenshots help explain the interface but do not replace functional evidence.

The research behind the design.

The report reviews electronic health records, patient portals, mobile health, appointments and reminders, AI, staff coordination, interoperability, privacy, and bilingual accessibility. Research helps explain the design choices; results from other systems are not results achieved by myhealth.

Records and patient portals

The literature discusses easier access to health information and the challenges of adoption, cost, digital skills, health literacy, and inconsistent outcome evidence. This supports testing a clear timeline and useful patient tools, without assuming they improve health outcomes.

Appointments and reminders

The report reviews missed-appointment studies and reminders, emphasizing that results vary by setting. Correct booking, verified reminder delivery, predictive performance, and an effective follow-up intervention require separate evaluation.

AI and staff coordination

The review considers errors, missing information, bias, misleading explanations, alert overload, and clear staff ownership. Fluent output alone is not evidence of medical accuracy. Professionals must retain responsibility for care decisions.

Interoperability, privacy, and usability

Compatible formats alone do not guarantee correct hospital record exchange. Patient matching, consent, terminology, provenance, permissions, security, and organizational approval matter. Bilingual and accessible interfaces also need evaluation with representative people.

Selected references named in the supplied documents:

  • Han et al. (2019) — patient portals
  • Zhao et al. (2017) — web-based medical appointments
  • Zaretsky et al. (2024) — patient-friendly medical summaries
  • Campanella et al. (2016) — electronic health records
  • Dantas et al. (2018) — appointment no-shows
  • Sutton et al. (2020) — clinical decision support
  • HL7 FHIR — a future interoperability direction

The complete reference lists are retained in the source-document text downloads below.

A plan built around steady development.

The proposal sets out a 16-week plan. The report describes iterative development, later integration and hardening, and repeated checks as the feature set grew. These weeks are planned stages, not verified completion dates.

  1. Weeks 1–3

    Understand the needs

    Collect requirements, identify user roles and research questions, and review related literature.

  2. Weeks 4–6

    Design the experience

    Plan the patient, staff, and administrator workflows, permissions, interface, and data relationships.

  3. Weeks 7–9

    Build and connect

    Implement the main screens, records, appointments, and clinical work; integrate supporting modules through later iterations.

  4. Weeks 10–12

    Test and review

    Check software rules, database changes, security boundaries, and selected end-to-end journeys.

  5. Weeks 13–16

    Document and present

    Reconcile the report with the implementation, record verification evidence, and prepare the demonstration and presentation.

Risks the report keeps in view

Data integrity, duplicate bookings, unauthorized record access, browser data exposure or loss, incomplete shared workflows, misleading AI claims, feature growth, monetary rounding, Arabic and accessibility issues, operational recovery, and unverified compliance claims. The proposed responses include focused scope, permission and retry tests, synthetic-only public data, explicit unavailable states, and reviewed deployment controls.

Where myhealth goes from here.

01

Strengthen the demonstration

Run the complete checks on the pinned toolchain, reconcile documentation, and verify key journeys in Arabic and English, including keyboard and enlarged-text use.

02

Complete the shared pilot

Finish missing remote workflows, verify two-device behavior and current permissions, and define a reviewed migration or import process.

03

Prepare responsible operations

Add approved private hosting, HTTPS, managed secrets, monitoring, off-host encrypted backups, and tested restoration.

04

Explore hospital connections

Work with a healthcare provider on HL7 FHIR, patient matching, consent, terminology, source history, and data quality. No connection is currently claimed.

05

Evaluate AI carefully

Check summaries against clinician-reviewed answers, test prediction calibration and fairness, and measure false alerts and staff workload before any operational use.

06

Extend patient services

Consider telehealth, verified reminders, medication follow-up, digital consent, and optional wearable measurements. Validate measurements and permissions before integration.

07

Measure usability and maintain quality

Run approved participant studies, record task time and errors, and maintain release notes, migration checks, API compatibility, and security reviews.

08

Grow storage when evidence supports it

Improve measured query performance and financial precision; consider larger storage or PostgreSQL only when capacity and real operational needs justify it.
